questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
For me, the most important thing when choosing a study destination was academic relevance. I knew quite early on that I wanted to move in the direction of social data science / computational social science, both because I’m interested in the field itself and because I plan to apply for the Master’s in Social Data Science at KU. So I really wanted an exchange where the courses would actually matter for that path, and not just be “nice to have”.

I spent quite a lot of time researching different universities and destinations, both in Europe and outside Europe, to see where you could study something close to social data science at bachelor level. I quickly realised that there are surprisingly few full bachelor programmes in this field. That’s why the University of Amsterdam stood out to me: it offers one of the first bachelor programmes in Europe fully focused on Computational Social Science. Even though the programme is still quite new, it felt like a unique chance to really explore the field and see how it works in practice.

Besides the academic side, the city itself mattered a lot. Amsterdam felt like a place where I would genuinely enjoy living for a semester. In many ways it reminded me of Copenhagen. That made it feel like a safe but still exciting choice, and it turned out to be a very nice place to live and spend everyday life.

I also considered options outside Europe, especially in the US, where there are strong academic environments in related fields. In the end, though, I’m very happy that I stayed in Europe and chose Amsterdam. Even if parts of the academic experience didn’t fully live up to my expectations, the overall experience – especially socially and personally – made it a really worthwhile exchange.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Overall, my exchange was an absolute blast, and I genuinely loved it. Coming home afterwards was surprisingly emotional, which I think says a lot about how meaningful the experience was for me. What really made the exchange special was the social and experiential side of it — meeting people, building friendships, living in a new city, and just being part of something different for a few months.

The reason I wouldn’t give the exchange a full 10 out of 10 is mainly because of the academic experience, which for me was more disappointing than expected. That said, I also realised quite quickly that an exchange is not primarily about academics. It’s about everything around it. The courses are part of the experience, but not the main reason you go — and once I accepted that, I enjoyed the exchange much more.

Academically, the programme I followed was very demanding in terms of time, with frequent small assignments, a lot of compulsory group work, and a very tight weekly structure. Personally, I found this quite frustrating at times, especially compared to what I was used to at KU. However, this didn’t take away from the overall experience in the end.

If I had to give one piece of advice, it would be: go on exchange for the people, the city, and the experience. If you do that, the exchange can be incredibly rewarding — and for me, it definitely was.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
Overall, it was very easy. The University of Amsterdam is extremely well organised when it comes to welcoming exchange students. If anything, there was almost too much information at times — but that’s definitely a good thing. I received a lot of emails and practical information before arrival, which meant that even if I felt a bit stressed beforehand, I always had what I needed.

Once I arrived, everything became much clearer. There were plenty of introductions and welcome activities, especially organised by ESN Amsterdam, which did a great job bringing exchange and international students together. There were social events, introductions, and even a big exchange party early on, which made it very easy to settle in and meet people.

I also got my housing through the University of Amsterdam, which made the arrival process much smoother. Overall, it really felt like a university that is very used to hosting exchange students and has strong structures in place to support them.

Personally, I didn’t need much help once I arrived, but it was very reassuring to know that support was always there. There are study advisers, international offices, student support services, psychologists, and even university doctors you can reach out to if needed. So even if things feel a bit overwhelming before the exchange starts, once you’re there you’re definitely not on your own.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I actually received quite a lot of support when I arrived, especially in the very beginning. The first thing was a two-day introduction organised by ESN (Erasmus Student Network), which focused mainly on social activities, getting to know other exchange and international students, and just having fun together. That was a really nice way to arrive, because it immediately gave a sense of community and made the first days feel much less overwhelming.

The week after, there was a more academic introduction day organised by the university, combined with additional social activities on the surrounding days. There was also a big welcome party, which was honestly a lot of fun and a great way to meet even more people early on.

In addition to the physical introductions, the university provided a lot of written information online — practical guides, emails, and resources you could read through at your own pace. I didn’t use everything, but it was reassuring to know that all the information was there if you needed it.

Housing was also a huge part of feeling supported. I was lucky enough to get housing through the university, which made arrival much easier and removed a lot of stress. I ended up living very centrally, right by the canals, and that honestly had a big positive impact on my exchange experience overall.

Looking back, I felt well taken care of when I arrived — both socially and practically — and it made settling into life in Amsterdam very smooth.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
For me, finding housing felt very easy — but I was also extremely lucky, and I want to be honest about that. I probably spent the least amount of time possible on housing and ended up with an almost unreal situation. I lived at Prinsengracht 225, right in the city centre, in a large student dorm with around 100 other exchange students. Everyone there was on exchange, which made the social side of living there absolutely amazing.

That said, I’m very aware that this was partly luck. I also met many regular (full-degree) students in Amsterdam who struggled much more with housing and often lived further outside the city. Housing in the Netherlands is generally difficult, especially in Amsterdam, and many students do have to compromise. Still, everyone I met did eventually find something.

My strongest recommendation is to use the University of Amsterdam’s housing lottery for exchange students and really give that a chance before trying to arrange anything yourself. That’s what I did, and it worked out incredibly well. Personally, I wouldn’t recommend committing to private housing before the lottery results are out. If you don’t get housing through the university, then you can start stressing and looking elsewhere — but until then, I’d wait.

I actually had a friend who tried to arrange private housing before the lottery and ended up renting a room in a private home, which was fine on paper but not at all comparable to the student housing experience. In the end, he even moved into student housing later on. Compared to that, living in a university-organised dorm with other exchange students made a huge difference for my overall exchange experience.

So in short: do the lottery, hope for the best, and only look elsewhere if it doesn’t work out. If you get university housing, it can really shape your exchange in the best possible way.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
At the University of Amsterdam, living off campus is basically the norm, especially within Social and Behavioural Sciences. As far as I know, there isn’t really student housing directly on the Roeterseiland campus where I studied, so everyone lives spread out across the city.

From my own experience, living off campus was actually one of the best parts of my exchange — mainly because of where and how I lived. I was in a student dorm with many other exchange students, and that honestly became the social core of my whole semester. Most of my closest friends from the exchange are people I met through my housing, and a lot of everyday social life happened there very naturally.

Living centrally also made a big difference. Being able to bike everywhere, live close to cafés, canals, and campus, and really feel part of the city was amazing. Amsterdam is extremely bike-friendly, and everyday life is very easy once you’re settled.

If I had to give one piece of advice, it would be: if you get the chance to live in a student dorm with other international or exchange students, take it. It makes it much easier to meet people, feel at home quickly, and get the most out of the social side of the exchange.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
If I could give one very concrete piece of advice to future exchange students going to Amsterdam, it would be about housing — and especially the university housing lottery.

My strongest recommendation is: do not start looking for private housing before you know the result of the University of Amsterdam housing lottery. Sign up for the lottery, follow all the emails and instructions carefully, and be patient. From what I remember, you sign up around May/June, and the results come out later in July, so it requires some calm nerves — but it’s absolutely worth it.

Once you sign up, you’ll be asked to choose between different price categories. Officially, UvA says that your choice doesn’t affect your chances. Whether that’s true or not, I can’t say — but I can share what I did. I chose category 3 (the second most expensive category), which mainly included private rooms. Importantly, this category also included Prinsengracht, where I ended up living. If you get the option, I would personally recommend choosing this category.

If you’re lucky and get a “winning number,” you’ll later receive an email with specific housing offers from a housing company (for me, this was Lieven de Key). This is the most important moment: check your email constantly. All students in the same category receive the offer at the same time, and rooms are booked on a first-come, first-served basis. When I received my offer, I saw it about 25 minutes late and literally dropped everything to book a room — luckily, there were still rooms available.

If you get the chance to book Prinsengracht, I would highly recommend it. Living there was honestly a huge reason why my exchange turned out as well as it did. It’s a large student dorm with only exchange students, very centrally located, and incredibly social. Most of my closest friends from the exchange lived there, and it really became the heart of my everyday life.

Some very specific (but optional) tips if you do get Prinsengracht:
	•	Garden-facing rooms are quieter than canal-facing rooms, which can have some street noise at night.
	•	First-floor rooms have very high ceilings and feel especially spacious.
	•	Third-floor rooms have lower ceilings, but nicer views.
	•	Ground-floor rooms are fine, but a few people experienced issues with mice (which can happen in Amsterdam).
	•	Most rooms are single rooms sharing a bathroom with one person of the same gender; there are only very few couple rooms.

Even if you don’t get Prinsengracht, many other university-organised housing options are also good. I just wanted to share this in detail because housing can completely shape your exchange experience, and for me, getting student housing through the university — and especially Prinsengracht — made my exchange as good as it possibly could have been.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
For me, the course registration process was very easy and straightforward. Once I understood how it worked, I didn’t really have any issues at all.

I personally knew very clearly which course I wanted to take in advance: the 30 ECTS first-semester course (“Foundations”) in Computational Social Science. Since it’s a full-semester package, registration was especially simple in my case. More generally, though, the University of Amsterdam has a well-structured system where you can easily look up all available courses before registering.

Course registration happens during a specific, relatively short time window, so the main thing is just to pay attention to the emails and make sure you register within those days. One nice thing is that you’re allowed to register for more ECTS than you actually plan to take. If you end up getting all the courses you registered for, you can simply deregister from the ones you don’t want afterwards. That gives you some flexibility and makes the process less stressful.

UvA also has a very good online timetable system (“Rooster”), where you can see all lectures, classes, and even exam dates in advance and build a visual schedule. Compared to KU, I found this system much clearer and easier to use, especially when trying to avoid clashes.

Overall, my experience was that as long as you read the information you receive and keep an eye on deadlines, course registration at UvA is smooth and well organised.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
There was actually a lot of help available, both before and during the exchange. First of all, you receive plenty of emails with practical information, and the University of Amsterdam’s website is very thorough. Almost everything you might need — from course registration to practical matters — can be found online if you take the time to look.

If there’s something you can’t figure out yourself, it’s very easy to get help. The International Office and study advisers are extremely approachable and helpful. I personally had quite a few questions for the International Office, and every time I contacted them, they were quick, kind, and very reassuring. It really felt like you were in safe hands.

Even once you’re there, you never feel left alone. I didn’t have any major issues myself, but I knew other exchange students who changed courses or adjusted their study plans during the semester, and they received plenty of support with that. I also know people who met with study advisers just to talk through their semester or plans, and they all had very positive experiences.

Overall, I never felt insecure or worried about not knowing what to do. There is always someone you can reach out to, and the university is genuinely good at helping exchange students — whether it’s about courses, planning, or practical issues.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I was completely successful. I knew very clearly which course I wanted to take — a single 30 ECTS course — so the registration process was very straightforward for me. I only registered for that course, even though it would have been possible to register for more, and I got in right away.

Everything went smoothly from the start, and I didn’t run into any issues at all. In my case, it was basically a 100% hit rate.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
My main advice would simply be to read the information you receive and follow the steps carefully. Everything you need is clearly explained in the emails and on the University of Amsterdam’s website, and if you stay on top of deadlines, the registration process is very manageable.

If you do run into any questions or uncertainties, don’t hesitate to reach out to the International Office or the study advisers. They are very approachable and genuinely helpful, and there’s a strong support system in place for exchange students. Even though I personally didn’t need much help, it was reassuring to know that assistance was always available if needed.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I want to add a short clarification regarding my relatively low satisfaction rating of the academic programme. The reason I rated it 2 out of 5 is very much related to the specific programme I chose, not the University of Amsterdam in general. Other exchange students following different programmes may (and likely will) have a very different academic experience.

I chose the first-semester Computational Social Science programme, and for me personally, it turned out to be academically disappointing — partly because I had very high expectations. UvA has a strong international reputation, and I expected a higher academic level, especially in relation to social science methods and theory.

One important factor was the workload structure. Compared to many other exchange students I met, I spent significantly more time on university work. The programme involved constant weekly deadlines, a lot of mandatory group work, and many scheduled workshops and lectures throughout the week. While this may suit some students, I found that the amount of time required was high relative to the academic learning I personally gained from it.

Another aspect was the student composition. Since exchange students can only join the first semester, most students in the programme were very young and had just started university. This is of course completely fine, but it did affect the academic dynamic, especially in group work. I was one of very few exchange students in a cohort that otherwise consisted of full-degree bachelor students, many of whom were new to both university life and social science.

Academically, I found the programme light on reading and theoretical depth. I was actually surprised by how little reading there was, and I often wished for fewer mandatory workshops and more time spent engaging deeply with texts and methods. Many sessions focused on completing tasks rather than developing a broader understanding of computational or social data science as a field.

That said, there were positive elements. I learned Python programming and developed stronger computational thinking skills, which I expect will be useful later on. Some instructors were very strong in technical areas, particularly programming. However, overall I felt that the programme did not fully meet my expectations in terms of social science methodology and academic depth.

In hindsight, I realised that exchange is not primarily about academics, and once I accepted that, my experience became much more enjoyable. Socially and personally, the exchange was an absolute highlight, and I would still strongly recommend going on exchange — just with careful consideration of programme choice, especially if academic depth is a priority for you.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
For the specific programme I followed, I personally found the academic level to be quite low, especially compared to my background and expectations. Since it was a first-semester bachelor programme, a large part of the curriculum focused on introductory social science methods that I was already very familiar with. As a result, much of the content felt repetitive to me, particularly in relation to qualitative research methods.

In practice, I found the coursework relatively easy, and I generally performed very well in the assignments. While that was of course nice, it also meant that I often felt under-challenged academically. I would have appreciated more depth, more reading, and more advanced discussions, especially given UvA’s strong academic reputation.

That said, I think it’s important to stress that this experience is highly programme-specific. Because exchange students can only join the first semester of this particular programme, the level was naturally adapted to students who had just started university. In that sense, the level makes sense — it just didn’t align very well with my own academic background and expectations.

From talking to other exchange students, I know that the academic level varies a lot across courses and programmes at UvA. Some exchange students found their courses very challenging, others found them manageable, and some found them easy. So my experience should not be taken as representative of UvA in general, but rather as something to keep in mind when choosing courses — especially if academic depth is a priority for you.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
This comparison is again very dependent on the specific programme and courses, so I can mainly speak from my own experience and what I learned from other exchange students.

In the Computational Social Science programme I followed, the teaching style was very workshop-based and attendance-heavy. There were many scheduled hours each week where you were expected to be physically present and actively working on tasks, often in groups. The semester was structured around two large projects, which was nice in principle, but it also meant continuous progress checks, weekly deliverables, and a lot of in-class work. Compared to UCPH, there was much less reading and much more focus on doing things during class time.

More generally, from talking to other exchange students at UvA, I got the impression that teaching there is often more structured and guided than at UCPH. There tends to be more compulsory activities, more continuous assessment, and in some courses sit-in exams or tests that focus on knowing specific content or details. This is quite different from sociology at UCPH, where we don’t have sit-in exams and where there is typically more emphasis on independent reading, essay writing, and broader analytical reflection.

Overall, I would say that the teaching style at UvA can feel a bit more school-like compared to UCPH — more attendance, more structure, and more continuous evaluation. That said, this varies a lot by course, and you can usually see the teaching and exam format in advance when choosing courses. Some students may really appreciate this structure, while others — especially those used to the UCPH style — might find it quite different.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: "FOUNDATION: Appreciating the complexity of social challenges” (course catalogue number 738100001Y)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I’ll be honest and say that I would only recommend the “Foundations” course (the first-semester Computational Social Science programme) if it really matches your preferences.

This course can be a good fit if you:
	•	enjoy having many scheduled classes and workshops
	•	like working actively during class time
	•	are comfortable with a lot of group work
	•	enjoy hands-on social science methods
	•	don’t mind relatively little reading, but a lot of compulsory in-class activities and continuous assignments

If that sounds appealing, then the course can work well. Personally, I would have preferred a more advanced academic level, more reading, and more theoretical depth, so it wasn’t the right fit for me academically — but that’s very subjective.

One thing I really want to highlight positively is the social and personal atmosphere of the programme. The learning teams are small, and I felt genuinely seen and appreciated as a student. I built very personal relationships with several lecturers and the programme study adviser, who were incredibly kind and supportive. There was a strong sense of community — including informal moments like coffee with lecturers, social gatherings, and even a shared end-of-semester dinner with staff and students. In that sense, the programme felt very warm and welcoming.

So overall, I wouldn’t recommend this course by default — but I would recommend it to students who actively want this specific teaching style and structure. If your priority is academic depth and independent study, I would suggest looking at other courses. If you value structure, community, and hands-on learning, this course might suit you well.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
I honestly didn’t encounter many unexpected costs. I biked everywhere, which made daily life very cheap and easy. I rarely used public transport, and I never really needed the metro.

Of course, if you want to travel around the Netherlands — for example to cities like Utrecht, Rotterdam, or Nijmegen — you’ll need to buy train tickets, but that’s easy to plan for and not really a surprise.

Many students rent a Swapfiets, which is very convenient, but I personally bought a second-hand bike for about €180, which worked perfectly for the whole semester (and I even brought it back to Denmark). Housing was by far the biggest expense, and aside from that, daily costs were quite manageable.

Overall, there were no major unexpected expenses, and living costs were pretty predictable once housing was sorted.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Overall, I found prices in Amsterdam to be quite similar to Copenhagen. Some things were slightly more expensive, others slightly cheaper, but on the whole the cost level felt familiar.

One thing that surprised me a bit was takeaway food. I rarely bought takeaway, but when I did, I found it relatively expensive — in some cases even more expensive than in Copenhagen. That might partly be because I lived very centrally, where there are many tourists, but things like pizza and other standard takeaway options were not particularly cheap.

For groceries, I mostly shopped at Albert Heijn and Jumbo. Albert Heijn can be quite pricey, but I would strongly recommend getting an Albert Heijn Bonus Card. The discounts make a huge difference, and they often have very good weekly or flash deals (sometimes 50% off on specific product categories). If you don’t mind the data tracking behind it, the Bonus Card really helps keep food costs down.

Another good tip is to buy items that are close to their expiration date. Albert Heijn uses dynamic discounts that can go up to 70% off, especially later in the day. If you’re flexible with what you cook, you can eat very cheaply this way.

Jumbo is generally a bit cheaper than Albert Heijn, and Lidl is also a good option if you live close to one. Personally, I found that with discounts and some flexibility, grocery shopping in Amsterdam was very manageable.

All in all, I didn’t experience any big price shocks — especially if you’re coming from Copenhagen, the price level feels quite comparable.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There were lots of options available if you wanted to get involved. The University of Amsterdam offers a wide range of sports and athletic activities through the university sports centre (USC), where you can join classes, gyms, and different sports clubs. I personally didn’t use this much, simply because I was already very busy socially and spent most of my time with friends.

Socially, there’s a lot going on. There are student cafés (for example on campus), where students often hang out after classes, grab a beer, and socialize. On top of that, ESN (Erasmus Student Network) is very active and organizes many events for exchange students, such as introductions, parties, bar crawls, trips, and other social activities. There are also smaller social events connected to specific programmes or student networks.

Overall, I’d say there are plenty of opportunities to be social, and it’s quite easy to meet people — especially as an exchange student.

One difference compared to UCPH is the party culture. UvA doesn’t really have the same kind of student-organised parties that we’re used to in Copenhagen. Most parties happen out in the city, at bars or venues, rather than being organised directly by students themselves. That said, Amsterdam has a huge nightlife, so depending on what you enjoy, there’s still a lot to do.

In short, there’s no lack of activities — it’s more about choosing what fits your interests and how social you want to be during your exchange.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
My biggest recommendation is to really prioritise the social side of the exchange. Explore the city, be curious, say yes to things, and focus on making friends. For me, the social life and experiences outside the university were by far the most important part of the exchange and what made it so memorable.

Amsterdam is an amazing city to live in as a student. Just biking around, discovering neighbourhoods, cafés, parks, museums, and different parts of the city is already a big part of the experience. I would really encourage future exchange students to spend time getting to know the city and not just sticking to their immediate area.

If you enjoy going out and dancing, I can very warmly recommend Skatecafé in Amsterdam Noord. It became our absolute go-to place during the exchange. It’s a very open-minded and welcoming venue with a great atmosphere and usually multiple dance floors with different types of music, depending on the night. The crowd is friendly, the vibe is relaxed, and it feels very unpretentious. Even though it’s a bit outside the city centre, it’s definitely worth the trip — just go a bit earlier in the evening to really enjoy it.

Beyond nightlife, there are also plenty of informal social activities organised through ESN and other student networks, which are great for meeting people, especially at the beginning of the exchange.

Overall, my advice would be: don’t overthink it. Be social, explore, and enjoy the freedom of being on exchange — those experiences are what you’ll remember long after the semester ends.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
My main recommendation is to take it weekend by weekend and be social. A lot of the best plans happen spontaneously, so I’d say follow the people around you, say yes to invitations, and just hang out together. That’s often how the most memorable weekends happen.

The Netherlands is very easy to explore. You can take the train almost anywhere, which makes day trips or short weekend trips very simple. I did a small road trip with friends where we visited smaller towns and villages around Amsterdam, including old canal towns, farming villages, and fishing towns — which was a really nice contrast to city life. We also travelled to places like Flevoland (reclaimed land) and Friesland, which gave a very different impression of the country.

Amsterdam itself also has amazing museums, neighbourhoods to explore, parks, cafés, and markets, so there’s always something to do even if you stay in the city. You’ll quickly get lots of recommendations from other students once you’re there.

Overall, I’d say: don’t overplan. Be open, travel a bit, explore locally, and enjoy spending time with the people you meet — that’s what makes weekends and holidays during exchange really special.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
My main recommendation is to take it weekend by weekend and be social. A lot of the best plans happen spontaneously, so I’d say follow the people around you, say yes to invitations, and just hang out together. That’s often how the most memorable weekends happen.

The Netherlands is very easy to explore. You can take the train almost anywhere, which makes day trips or short weekend trips very simple. I did a small road trip with friends where we visited smaller towns and villages around Amsterdam, including old canal towns, farming villages, and fishing towns — which was a really nice contrast to city life. We also travelled to places like Flevoland (reclaimed land) and Friesland, which gave a very different impression of the country.

Amsterdam itself also has amazing museums, neighbourhoods to explore, parks, cafés, and markets, so there’s always something to do even if you stay in the city. You’ll quickly get lots of recommendations from other students once you’re there.

Overall, I’d say: don’t overplan. Be open, travel a bit, explore locally, and enjoy spending time with the people you meet — that’s what makes weekends and holidays during exchange really special.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
I personally spent most of my time socialising with other exchange students, especially the people in my student dorm, simply because we were in the same situation and very like-minded. That said, there were plenty of opportunities to socialise with local (Dutch) students as well, especially within my programme.

My main tip would simply be: approach people and talk to them. Dutch students are generally very kind, open, and welcoming. They can sometimes come across as quite direct in the way they communicate, but that’s just part of the culture and usually meant in a friendly and honest way.

If you actively want to meet more local students, it helps to take part in programme-related activities, group work, or student events. ESN events, bar crawls, cafés, and other social gatherings are also good places to meet both local and international students. Even though I didn’t personally feel the need to seek this out much — since I already had a very active social life — the opportunities were definitely there.

Overall, I don’t think socialising with local students is difficult if you’re open, curious, and willing to take the first step.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
I didn’t find any cultural differences particularly challenging overall. The environment was very international, especially within my programme, and people came from many different cultural backgrounds. Because of that, you naturally encounter different ways of communicating, behaving, and working together.

At times, you could notice that people were used to different academic or social norms, which is completely normal in an international setting. I don’t think this ever led to any real clashes — it just requires being open-minded, patient, and aware that not everyone shares the same cultural references or expectations.

One small thing to be aware of is that Danish humour and sarcasm don’t always translate well, so it can be useful to be a bit more mindful of how things might be interpreted. But overall, I experienced the cultural diversity as a positive thing rather than a challenge.

In general, as long as you approach differences with curiosity and kindness, it’s very easy to adapt and enjoy the international atmosphere.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
One of the things I appreciated most was how direct and honest Dutch people are in the way they communicate. In many ways, it felt quite similar to Danish culture, which made it very easy for me to adapt and feel at home quickly.

I also really loved the biking culture. Being able to bike everywhere — to university, to friends, to cafés, and around the city in general — made everyday life both easy and enjoyable. It felt very natural and familiar, especially coming from Copenhagen.

Overall, I found Dutch culture very easy to connect with, and I didn’t experience any major culture shock. The similarities to Danish culture made the whole exchange feel comfortable from the beginning, while still being exciting and new.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange?
	1.	Prioritise the social experience.
Be social, say yes to things, and don’t stress too much about the academics. Of course, you can and should try to learn something — but if you feel demotivated academically or find the level different from what you’re used to, that’s completely okay. When the exchange is over, it’s the people you met, the experiences you had, and the memories you made that will matter the most.
	2.	Go all in on the university housing lottery.
Do everything you can to participate in the University of Amsterdam’s housing lottery and be patient with the process. If you get the chance, I would strongly recommend choosing category 3 and, if offered, Prinsengracht. Also: check your email constantly during the booking period — housing offers are first come, first served, and timing really matters.
	3.	Be present and enjoy the time — it goes by fast.
The semester passes incredibly quickly. Take time to reflect, enjoy everyday moments, and remember to take photos and appreciate where you are. Don’t rush through it — just be present, make memories, and enjoy the experience while it lasts.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
If there’s one thing I would really emphasise, it’s student housing. I’ve already written about this earlier, but it’s worth repeating: go for the University of Amsterdam student housing lottery. Don’t panic too early and don’t try to secure private housing before you know the outcome of the lottery. Follow the instructions carefully, be patient, and see if you get lucky. Only after you know the result should you start looking for other housing options if necessary.

Beyond housing, my general advice would be to remember that there are a lot of people at the university who are there to help you. Whether it’s the International Office, study advisers, or other support services, don’t hesitate to reach out if you have questions or uncertainties. From my experience, they are very responsive, kind, and helpful — and you’re never expected to figure everything out on your own.

Overall, if you stay on top of emails, follow instructions, and ask for help when needed, the practical side of going on exchange to UvA is very manageable.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Without a doubt, the most rewarding part was the social experience — making friends, sharing everyday life, and creating memories together. Looking back now, that’s what really matters to me.

While the academic part didn’t fully meet my expectations, that honestly doesn’t matter in hindsight. What stays with me are the friendships I made, the moments we shared, and the experiences we had together in Amsterdam. Those memories mean a lot to me, and they’re something I’ll carry with me for a long time.

I wouldn’t change my exchange for anything. It was an incredibly special time, and I’m very grateful for it.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
I didn’t experience any major personal challenges or difficult situations during the exchange. Overall, things went very smoothly. The main challenge for me was academic frustration, which I’ve mentioned earlier. I spent quite a lot of time on coursework that didn’t always feel very motivating or rewarding, and that could be demotivating at times.

What helped was accepting that this feeling was okay and reminding myself that exchange is about much more than academics. Once I shifted my focus and allowed myself to prioritise the social experience and everyday life, things became much easier and more enjoyable.

Interestingly, something very positive also came out of this challenge. Because the programme had close interaction with lecturers, I was able to get a short-term research assistant position with a professor during the semester. Through that, I worked on advanced quantitative and econometric modelling and learned a lot academically — much more than I had expected from the programme itself. It ended up being a really valuable and motivating experience, and it showed me that even when parts of the exchange are frustrating, unexpected opportunities can arise.

Looking back, the challenge was real, but it also helped me grow and led to experiences I wouldn’t otherwise have had.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
Nothing more to add, apart from repeating how important housing is. If you take anything from this report, let it be the advice about the University of Amsterdam housing lottery, which I’ve described in detail above. That’s where my experience can hopefully be most useful for future exchange students.

Other than that, enjoy it — exchange is something very special.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
